extraction.research_question: How can an agent learn by trial-and-error interaction with an environment to maximize cumulative reward, and what are the key ideas and algorithms for doing so (stated aim: a clear and simple account of the key ideas and algorithms of reinforcement learning, per the Preface to the Second Edition)?
extraction.theory: Markov decision process framework with Bellman equations for value functions (Chapters 3-4); temporal-difference learning (Chapter 6); eligibility traces (Chapter 12); policy gradient methods (Chapter 13); links to animal psychology and neuroscience reward prediction error hypotheses (Chapters 14-15).
extraction.data: No empirical dataset. Simulated 10-armed bandit testbed (2000 randomly generated bandit problems, 1000 time steps each, averaged over 2000 runs) and simulated random-walk and gridworld tasks. Chapter 16 case studies report results from prior work, mainly games (backgammon, checkers, Go, Jeopardy! wagering) and computer systems (memory controller, video games).
extraction.method: Expository textbook with worked examples, pseudocode, exercises and mathematical derivations (optional material in shaded boxes). Simulation experiments compare algorithms, for example greedy versus epsilon-greedy action-value methods on the 10-armed testbed.
extraction.measures: Average reward per step on the 10-armed testbed; RMS error on the random-walk prediction task (Chapter 6); win outcomes and Elo ratings in Go; percentage speed improvement in the memory controller study; estimated probability of winning in TD-Gammon.
extraction.scope: Single-agent sequential decision problems modeled as Markov decision processes or bandits, mainly tabular methods first and then function approximation. Field is artificial intelligence and machine learning, not social science. Relevance to lobbying, elections, persuasion, turnout, networks or text measurement: none of these topics appears in the text. Closest overlaps are bandit and contextual-bandit allocation (Sections 2.9 and 16.7).
key_findings: Section 2.3 (pp. 28-30): On the 10-armed testbed (2000 random bandit problems, 1000 steps, 2000 runs), the greedy method reaches about 1 reward per step against a best possible of about 1.54, and performs significantly worse in the long run because it gets stuck on suboptimal actions.
Section 11.3 (p. 264): The deadly triad of function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy training, combined, can cause instability and divergence in the prediction case.

Section 16.1 (pp. 421-429): TD-Gammon combined TD(lambda) with a multilayer neural network trained on self-play. TD-Gammon 0.0 with essentially zero backgammon knowledge learned to play approximately as well as the best previous backgammon computer after about 300,000 self-play games.
Section 16.1: Adding specialized backgammon features while keeping self-play TD learning produced TD-Gammon 1.0, described as clearly substantially better than all previous backgammon programs.
Section 16.1: The backgammon game tree has an effective branching factor of about 400, too large for conventional heuristic search methods used in chess and checkers.

Section 16.3 (pp. 429-432): Watson Daily-Double wagering used a TD-Gammon-style value function learned over millions of simulated games and chose the bet with the maximum action value. The cited authors report its effectiveness went well beyond what human players do in live play.

Section 16.4 (pp. 429-432): A reinforcement learning memory controller improved on the FR-FCFS controller by 7 percent to 33 percent across nine applications, averaging 19 percent, and closed 27 percent of the gap to an unrealizable Optimistic controller, per the text.

Section 16.6.2 (p. 447): AlphaGo Zero trained over 4.9 million self-play games in about 3 days. In a 100-game match it defeated the AlphaGo version that beat Lee Sedol in all 100 games. Reported Elo ratings: 4308 for AlphaGo Zero, 3739 for the Lee Sedol version, 3144 for the Fan Hui version.
Section 16.7 (p. 450): Personalized delivery of news or advertisements is framed as a contextual bandit problem, because a non-associative bandit does not personalize content delivery.
Chapter 1 (pp. 8-13): The tic-tac-toe example learns position value estimates from self-play using a temporal-difference style update; this is the book framing example for the core RL idea.
extraction.limitations: Preface: the book is an introduction and makes no attempt at comprehensive coverage of a field that has exploded in many directions. It avoids a rigorous formal treatment, keeping the more mathematical parts in shaded boxes. Focus is on core online learning algorithms. Chapter 16 includes only a handful of applications, out of necessity.

summary_md: Sutton and Barto's second edition is the standard textbook on reinforcement learning (RL): an agent learns a policy by trial and error so as to maximize cumulative reward. It moves from k-armed bandits and the exploration-exploitation trade-off (Ch. 2), through finite MDPs, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo and temporal-difference learning (Ch. 3-7), to model-based planning (Ch. 8), function approximation and the deadly triad (Ch. 9-11), eligibility traces, policy gradients, psychology and neuroscience, and case studies (Ch. 16). It contains no social-science data. Its evidence is simulation (on the 10-armed testbed, greedy averages about 1 reward per step against a best of about 1.54) plus reported applications: TD-Gammon after about 300,000 self-play games, AlphaGo Zero after 4.9 million self-play games, and Adobe ad policies scored by high-confidence off-policy evaluation on bank-website logs. For Paul's systems the book is mainly vocabulary and foundation, not evidence. It underlies the RL influence-maximization papers in the vault (Chen 2021 and 2023, RELINK) that Paul maps to the seed gate and the allocator. Measured against the code, the joint CU optimizer is a one-shot, model-based plan. It runs greedy against modeled flip probabilities, never explores, and ingests no observed outcomes (observations=[]). It replans only after modeled threshold crossings. In the book's terms it is pure exploitation of a fixed model, with a myopic single-period objective. The book also sharpens a feasibility limit on Paul's expectation that a learned policy will replace greedy. Its successes needed hundreds of thousands to millions of episodes, but a real CU allocation gives roughly one episode per two-year cycle. Any learned policy would therefore be trained inside the same unvalidated simulator. Section 16.7 points to the more transferable idea: evaluate a candidate allocation policy off-policy from logged contacts and funding, with propensities. The prospective contract does not do this.

bearings.paper_claim: Acting greedily on current value estimates without exploration can lock onto suboptimal actions. On the 10-armed testbed (2000 independent problems, 1000 steps each), the greedy method averages about 1 reward per step against a best possible of about 1.54, and epsilon-greedy does better in the long run. Planning on an incorrect model is likely to compute a suboptimal policy (Sec. 8.3); planning uses a model, learning from experience uses observed interactions (Sec. 8.1).
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 2.2-2.3, pp. 27-30; Sec. 8.1, pp. 159-161; Sec. 8.3 (When the Model Is Wrong)
bearings.system_side: fec/engine/optimize.py allocates a CU budget (default $2.5M in $500 increments, with a per-member cap PMAX) by lazy greedy on modeled marginals of flip_value. The loop stops at the budget or when no positive marginal remains, so spend can fall short of the pot. It has no exploration term. observations is an empty list reserved for real outcomes. It replans after a modeled defection threshold is crossed (the conversions list), so it is not a one-shot plan. In RL terms it is greedy exploitation of a modeled response with no feedback from observed outcomes.

extraction.venue: ICML (International Conference on Machine Learning); venue line not printed in the extracted text, hint kept from item
extraction.coverage: Full extracted text read in two chunks (about 10,024 lines): abstract, introduction, preliminaries, shaping rewards, main results (theorem, corollary, remarks), experiments, discussion, acknowledgments, references, Appendix A (necessity proof). Reward design, value functions, goal-reaching path tasks and multi-step learning were all read. The paper has no lobbying, network, allocation, election, persuasion, turnout, legislator or text-measurement content. Page images not rendered. Paul annotations: none (item lists n_annots 0 and annot_sha12s empty; no _annots file exists for sha12 94066dc12fe3), so paul_markup is empty. Extraction drops ligatures and some digits, so the learning rate, epsilon, slip probabilities, number of runs and the Manhattan scaling constant are unreadable and left out.
extraction.research_question: Under what conditions can the reward function of a finite Markov decision process be modified (reward shaping) without changing which policies are optimal, especially when the learner does not know the transition function or the original reward?
extraction.theory: Bellman optimality for finite MDPs (discounted, and undiscounted with an absorbing goal state). A shaping reward F(s,a,s prime) is added to the original reward R. The paper defines potential-based shaping F(s,a,s prime) = gamma*Phi(s prime) - Phi(s) for an arbitrary real function Phi on states.
extraction.data: No empirical dataset. Simulated grid-world MDPs: a shortest-path goal task on a 10x10 grid, the same task on a 50x50 grid, and a 5x5 grid in which five subgoals (flags) must be visited in order before the final goal. Start and goal are in opposite corners for the goal-only grids. Unit of analysis: learning trial and steps taken to reach the goal. Number of independent runs used for averaging is not recoverable from the extraction.
extraction.method: Formal analysis: definitions, a sufficiency proof (potential-based F leaves optimal policies unchanged, with Q and V shifted by Phi), a necessity proof for the case of no prior knowledge of T and R (Appendix A, fully worked for finite states and two actions), and robustness remarks. Simulation: Sarsa and Sarsa(lambda) with epsilon-greedy exploration on the grid worlds, comparing no shaping against shaping with a Manhattan-distance potential and, in the subgoal task, a subgoal-count potential and a fine-tuned estimate of V*.
extraction.scope: Finite-state, finite-action MDPs with deterministic, bounded rewards. The paper argues infinite-state results follow under suitable regularity conditions but defers those proofs to a full version. Era: 1999 reinforcement-learning practice. Population: learning agents in small simulated domains; no real-world system.
extraction.measures: Steps taken to reach the goal per trial (learning curves). Theoretical objects: optimal Q-function, optimal value V*, and shaped Q and V. No statistical tests are reported.
key_findings: Potential-based shaping F(s,a,s prime) = gamma*Phi(s prime) - Phi(s) is sufficient: every optimal policy of the shaped MDP is optimal in the original MDP, and vice versa. Location: Main results, Theorem, sufficiency part and its proof.

Necessity: absent prior knowledge of T and R, potential-based F is the only shaping form that guarantees consistency with the optimal policy; for any non-potential F there exist transitions and rewards such that no optimal policy of the shaped MDP is optimal in the original. Location: Main results, Theorem, necessity part; proof in Appendix A (finite states, two actions).

Corollary: Q prime*(s,a) = Q*(s,a) - Phi(s) and V prime*(s) = V*(s) - Phi(s), so the shaped problem has the same argmax over actions. With Phi zero at the absorbing state the identities hold exactly in the undiscounted case. Location: Main results, Corollary.

Robustness remark: the identities hold for arbitrary policies, not only optimal ones, so near-optimal policies are also preserved and an epsilon-optimal policy learned on the shaped MDP is epsilon-optimal in the original. Location: Main results, Remark (Robustness and learning).

Remark: if the original reward is itself potential-based, every policy is optimal in the original MDP, so potential-based shaping gives no reason to prefer one policy over another. Location: Main results, Remark (All policies optimal under potential).

Choosing Phi = V*(s) makes the shaped optimal value function identically zero, which the authors describe as an easy function to learn, leaving only the non-zero Q-values to learn. Location: Main results, paragraph after the Corollary.

On the 10x10 goal grid, a Manhattan-distance potential speeds learning substantially; on the 50x50 grid, unshaped learning is far slower, with the authors saying it is losing hopelessly to the potential-based version. Location: Experiments, first two grid-world figures; the step axes run to about 600 (10x10) and about 2.5 x 10^4 (50x50).

Even a crude potential (zero, or a distance-based estimate) still helps the early phase of learning, while the finely tuned V*-based potential does better still. Location: Experiments, first grid-world discussion.

Subgoal task (5x5 grid, five flags visited in order): a potential that counts achieved subgoals, scaled by an expected time per subgoal, gives a reward jump at each subgoal and speeds learning clearly over no shaping; the fine-tuned V*-estimate potential performs better still. Location: Experiments, subgoal figure and text; the trial axis runs to about 450 and the step axis to about 800.

Non-potential shaping can create positive-return cycles: in the bicycle example (Randlov and Alstrom), an agent rewarded for progress toward the goal but not penalized for moving away learned to ride in tiny circles; a soccer robot rewarded for touching the ball learned to stay next to it and vibrate. Location: Introduction and Shaping rewards section.

Discussion: the authors suggest that non-potential shaping may still help in practice when used with care, but carries no guarantee; learning a rough shaping function as a multiscale value-function approximation is named as promising future work. Location: Discussion and Conclusions.

Extensions stated without full proof: for semi-MDPs with variable action durations tau the potential form generalizes to F = gamma^tau*Phi(s prime) - Phi(s); policy-class-restricted learning also preserves the guarantee; positive rescaling of rewards is allowed. Location: Discussion and Conclusions; Shaping rewards section.
limitations: Fully rigorous proofs only for finite state spaces; infinite-state extensions are asserted, with bounded shaping rewards required, and the full proofs are deferred to a longer paper.
Necessity proof is given in full only for two actions; the general case is described as obvious but tedious.
The guarantee covers optimal policies under the stated assumptions; for undiscounted problems with non-potential shaping the authors concede no general guarantee.

Empirics are limited to small simulated grid worlds and a subgoal task; there is no real-world or high-dimensional domain, no statistical tests, and the number of runs is not recoverable from the extraction.
Only Sarsa and Sarsa(lambda) are tested; there is no comparison with other shaping schemes or with learned shaping functions.
Non-potential shaping is discussed qualitatively; the paper does not quantify its harm or benefit.

summary_md: Ng, Harada and Russell (ICML 1999) ask which additions to an MDP reward leave the optimal policy unchanged. Their answer is potential-based shaping, F(s,a,s') = gamma*Phi(s') - Phi(s). It is sufficient for any real Phi on states. It is also necessary when nothing is known about the transitions or the reward: for any other F there is some MDP in which the shaped optimum is wrong. The corollary is that shaped Q and V equal the originals minus Phi(s), so the argmax over actions is the same. When Phi = V*, the shaped value is zero and greedy one-step choice is already optimal. A robustness remark adds that near-optimal policies carry over too. The experiments are small Sarsa grid worlds (10x10, 50x50, and a 5x5 grid with five subgoals). The paper reports no statistical tests, and this extraction lost the run counts. None of Paul's systems is a reinforcement learner. The bearing is on path-finding, where the deterministic case with gamma = 1 is the same thing as A* reduced costs, c'(u,v) = c(u,v) - h(u) + h(v). The theorem gives the rule for the learned or landmark heuristic Paul wants (his staffer and recruitment routers use heuristic 0 today). The heuristic must enter as a potential and be consistent; any other additive bonus changes which route wins. The staffer router's terminal normalization is a constant shift and is safe. Its member-context modifier and balanced step penalty change routes, which is correct as long as they are described as objective changes. One finding: the cosponsor recruitment path follows a greedy rule over a distance-to-target table that ignores dropped members. The template still calls this path provably optimal. UNVERIFIED until reproduced.

bearings.paper_claim: Corollary: shaped Q' = Q - Phi and V' = V - Phi, with Phi(absorbing) = 0 in the undiscounted case, so the shaped and original problems share the same argmax over actions. Remark (Robustness and learning): the identities hold for arbitrary policies, so an epsilon-accurate potential keeps policies epsilon-near-optimal. Choosing Phi = V* makes V' identically zero, which the authors call an easy value function to learn.
bearings.paper_location: Main results: Corollary; Remark (Robustness and learning); paragraph after the Corollary on Phi = V*
bearings.system_side: buildPath (line 753) calls distToTarget(target) (line 734), a max-product proximity over the full PE graph that does not exclude dropped members. tracePath (line 740) takes the argmax of PE[cur][v] times dT[v] over unseen, non-dropped neighbours. With no drops this greedy step is exact because dT satisfies the Bellman equation. With a drop, dT still counts paths through the dropped member, so the greedy step can follow a dead end or a weaker chain. The comment at line 735 says PROVABLY-OPTIMAL and is wrong once a member is dropped. A toy replica of these functions (scratchpad folder ng1999, file trap2.js) gave chain product 0.009 where the best drop-avoiding chain is 0.36 (case 1), and reached=false while a path exists (case 2). This replicates the logic only, not the browser page.

The paper does not discuss A*, heuristics used in search, or bidirectional search.

bearings.system_side: staffer_routing.py:386 and staffer_closeness_routes.py:79 both state Bidirectional Dijkstra with heuristic 0, with terminal costs and a virtual sink (search code from line 511). No heuristic is in use. The theorem covers changing the objective (rewards or arc costs). A search heuristic in A* changes search effort, not the objective, so it lies outside the theorem. Its correctness depends on admissibility or consistency, which is standard A* theory and not in this paper. The potential condition applies only if a heuristic is folded into arc costs as a reweighting, where telescoping keeps route ranking.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Holds for deterministic additive costs. Bidirectional search, the 10^12 tie band and Yen ranking are outside the paper and need their own checks in original cost units. extraction.coverage: Full text read in one chunk (28,661 chars): front matter, abstract, sections 1-4, appendix (action-replay process, Lemmas A and B, B.1-B.4), notes, references. Paper is purely theoretical, so there are no data or empirical sections. extraction.research_question: Under what conditions does Q-learning, an incremental model-free method for learning optimal action-values in controlled Markov processes, converge to the optimal Q values?
extraction.data: None. Theoretical paper. Setting is a finite discrete controlled Markov process with finite state and action sets and bounded rewards; no sample, unit, N or period.
extraction.method: Formal convergence proof. An artificial action-replay process (ARP) is built from the episode sequence. Lemma A (p.282, proof p.288) shows the Q_n values are optimal ARP action values, by backward induction. Lemma B (p.282-284, appendix p.289-291) has four parts: B.1 discounting of infinite sequences, B.2 probability of straying below a level, B.3 stochastic convergence of ARP transition and reward estimates via Kushner and Clark (1978), B.4 close rewards and transitions imply close values. Section 3.2 (p.284-285) combines these with epsilon bounds on s-step values.
extraction.theory: Dynamic programming and Bellman optimality; Sutton's temporal differences (TD); stochastic approximation (Kushner and Clark 1978).
extraction.identification: Not statistical identification. Convergence holds with probability 1 under: every state and action tried infinitely often (p.281); bounded rewards; discount 0 < gamma < 1; learning rates 0 < alpha_n < 1 satisfying conditions on their sums and sums of squares (equation 3, formula garbled in extraction, p.282-283).
extraction.scope: Finite discrete Markov decision processes with a look-up table representation of Q values; bounded rewards; discounting. Section 4 sketches (does not prove) two extensions: undiscounted processes with absorbing goal states (p.285-286), and updating many Q values per iteration (p.286). Excluded: function approximation and multi-step updates such as TD(lambda) (p.286). Era: 1992, following Watkins (1989).
extraction.measures: Action-value Q(x,a): expected discounted reward for action a in state x followed by a policy thereafter (p.280). Convergence criterion: Q_n(x,a) tends to Q*(x,a) for all x,a with probability 1 as n tends to infinity. Bounds on value differences grow at most quadratically in the number of actions s (p.283).
key_findings: Theorem (p.282): with bounded rewards, learning rates in (0,1) meeting the stated conditions, and all state-action pairs sampled infinitely often, Q_n(x,a) converges to Q*(x,a) for all x and a, with probability 1. Section 3.2, p.284-285.
Lemma A (p.282, appendix p.288): the Q_n values are the optimal action values of the ARP at every level n, proved by induction on n.
Lemma B.3 (p.283-284, appendix p.290): ARP transition probabilities and expected rewards converge with probability 1 to those of the real process as the level grows.

B.4 (p.283, appendix p.291): if transitions and rewards of s chained steps are within eta of the true values, the value of the s actions differs by at most a term growing quadratically in s, so close models give close values.
B.1 (p.283, appendix p.289): with discount gamma below 1 and bounded rewards, the effect of truncating an infinite sequence after s actions tends to 0 as s grows.

Section 4 (p.285-286): the theorem extends to undiscounted processes with absorbing goal states, because a bound on steps to trap and a minimum trap probability replace discounting. Sketched, not fully proved.
Section 4 (p.286): updating many Q values per iteration preserves convergence with no non-trivial change to the proof, since the ARP still estimates the same quantities from more episodes.

Section 4 (p.286): reusing stored episodes interpolates between Q-learning and certainty equivalence; in the limit of re-presenting old episodes infinitely often, reuse equals the certainty-equivalence step on the observed sample.

Section 4 (p.286): the proof covers only a restricted form of Watkins (1989) because it does not allow updates from rewards of more than one iteration; the TD(lambda) extension does not follow trivially and may need other proof methods.
limitations: Look-up table representation only; Watkins (1989) shows convergence may fail for other representations (p.282).
Requires an infinite number of episodes for each starting state and action (p.281-282). The authors call this strong but argue no method could do better under the stochastic conditions.
Convergence is asymptotic (n tends to infinity) with probability 1; no rates or finite-sample bounds are given.
Undiscounted and multi-update cases are sketched only (p.285-286).
Multi-step (TD(lambda)-style) updates are not covered by the proof (p.286).

Assumes the set of available actions is the same in every state; the authors note in footnote 1 that the general case extends straightforwardly.

summary_md: Watkins and Dayan (Machine Learning 8, 1992, pp. 279-292) give the convergence proof for one-step Q-learning, a model-free way to learn optimal action values in a finite controlled Markov process. The theorem (p.282) says Q_n(x,a) converges to Q*(x,a) with probability 1 if rewards are bounded, learning rates sit in (0,1) with divergent sums and finite sums of squares, values are kept in a lookup table, and every state-action pair is tried infinitely often. The proof builds an artificial action-replay process from the episode history. Lemma A shows Q_n is optimal for that process. Lemma B shows the process converges to the real one. Section 4 sketches two extensions: undiscounted problems with absorbing goal states, and updating many Q values per step. It also notes that replaying stored episodes moves the method toward certainty-equivalence planning. The proof gives no convergence rate and no finite-sample bound. It does not cover function approximation, which the authors say may fail to converge (p.282), or multi-step TD(lambda) updates. For Paul's systems this is background rather than a method in use. The repo has no reinforcement learning. The joint optimizer is a certainty-equivalence planner. It takes a modeled stance state and runs exact greedy allocation over it, and its list for observed outcomes is empty. The paper matters for one point: Paul expects a learned policy such as GCOMB to replace greedy allocation at scale. GCOMB and S2V-DQN use Q-learning with function approximation, which is outside this theorem. A lobbying cycle also cannot try each member-action pair the many times the theorem requires. An online scan found no applications of RL to lobbying or to allocating contributions across legislators.

Section 4 (p.286) says reusing stored episodes moves Q-learning toward certainty-equivalence planning, which is the limit of re-presenting old episodes infinitely often. Certainty equivalence costs dearly early in learning, citing Barto and Singh 1990 (p.280).

extraction.title: Learning Combinatorial Optimization Algorithms over Graphs
extraction.document_type: Conference paper (NeurIPS 2017), read from the arXiv v4 text
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all of the main body (Sections 1-6), Appendix A-B, and Appendix C-D including Tables C.1-C.2 and D.1-D.9, in chunks from line 1 to line 2988 of the text file. Tables D.1-D.8 (generalization grids) were skimmed for their headline pattern rather than every cell. Front matter, abstract, intro, method (Sections 2-4), experiments (Section 5, Tables 2-3), and appendices on instance generation, SCP, realistic data and hyperparameters were all read. Touched by topic: network diffusion and influence spread (MVC on MemeTracker, Appendix C.1 and C.4), path-finding and routing (TSP, MVC/MaxCut as graph heuristics). No lobbying, elections, persuasion, turnout, legislators or text-measurement content. Paul markup: the item lists zero annotation sha12s and no paul_entries, so no _annots files exist to read. Page images not rendered; text only. Metadata check: title, authors, year and venue hints are correct per the text and an online scan (NeurIPS proceedings page, arXiv). doi left empty since neither the text nor the scan supplies one. Online scan confirmed the NeurIPS 2017 venue and the arXiv v4 date; the PDF was already present in _raw, so no new download was made.
extraction.research_question: Can heuristics for NP-hard graph combinatorial optimization problems be learned automatically from a distribution of instances that share structure, rather than hand-designed with trial and error? (Abstract; Introduction p.2)
extraction.theory: Greedy meta-algorithm: a feasible solution is built by successively adding nodes chosen by an evaluation function Q, with the problem supplied through a helper function, cost function and termination criterion (Section 2). Reinforcement learning view: states are partial solutions, actions add a node, rewards are changes in the cost (Section 4.1, Table 1). No economic or political theory; the framing is algorithm design and ML.
extraction.data: Synthetic: Erdos-Renyi (edge probability 0.15) and Barabasi-Albert (average degree 4) graphs for MVC and MaxCut, with node counts sampled from ranges such as 15-20 up to 1000-1200 (Sections 5 and D.1); 2-D Euclidean TSP instances (random and clustered) from the DIMACS generator, unit is one graph or tour instance, training sets of 100 held-out validation graphs and 1000 test graphs (Section 5). Set covering built from the MemeTracker diffusion graph (Appendix B and C.4). Realistic: MemeTracker network of 960 nodes and 5000 edges for MVC (Appendix C.1, diffusion probabilities from average transmission times with alpha 0.1); ten Ising spin-glass MaxCut instances, 125 nodes and 375 edges each, from the optsicom MaxCut library (Appendix C.2); 38 TSPLIB instances from 51 to 318 cities (Appendix C.3). Period: not applicable; no calendar data.
extraction.method: Structure2vec graph embedding (T about 4 to 5 message-passing rounds, embedding size p = 64) feeds a Q-function approximation for a greedy policy (Sections 3.1-3.2, Table D.9). Training uses n-step Q-learning combined with fitted Q-iteration over an experience replay buffer, with epsilon annealed from 1.0 to 0.05 (Section 4.2, Algorithm 1, Appendix D.5). Testing uses the deterministic greedy policy, not Active Search, except for TSPLIB where Active Search is applied on each instance (Sections 5 and C.3). Baselines: MVCApprox and MVCApprox-Greedy, MaxcutApprox and SDP, TSP heuristics (Farthest, Cheapest, Closest, Christofides, 2-opt, Nearest, MST), pointer networks with actor-critic (PN-AC, reimplemented), and CPLEX for optimal or best-known solutions with a 1-hour cutoff.
extraction.identification: None in the econometric sense. Generalization is tested by training on one size range (50-100 nodes for the headline generalization table) and testing on larger graphs up to 1200 nodes (Section 5.2, Table 2). Performance is judged by approximation ratio against CPLEX or Concorde best-known values, averaged over test instances (Section 5).
extraction.scope: Graph combinatorial optimization on synthetic and a few public benchmark graphs. Population: NP-hard graph problems MVC, MaxCut, TSP and set covering. Era: NeurIPS 2017 (arXiv 2017, revised 2018). Not an institutional or political study.
extraction.measures: Approximation ratio R(S,G) = max(OPT/c, c/OPT) averaged over test instances (Section 4 preamble of Section 5). Running time on a single GPU, and the time-approximation trade-off compared with CPLEX solutions over time (Section 5.3, Figure 3). Cut weight and tour cost in the realistic tables (Tables C.1, C.2).
key_findings: On 1000 synthetic test graphs the approximation ratio of S2V-DQN is very close to 1 for MVC and beats MVCApprox, MVCApprox-Greedy, PN-AC and all TSP heuristics on most settings (Section 5.1, Figure 2).

Generalization: trained on 50-100 node graphs, S2V-DQN gives MVC (BA) ratio 1.0062 and MaxCut (BA) ratio 1.0038 on 1000-1200 node graphs (Section 5.2, Table 2); TSP clustered ratio rises to 1.1065 at that size.
Speed: on 1200-node graphs MVC is solved in about 11 seconds on one GPU at ratio 1.0062 (Section 5.3); MVC is slightly slower than the approximation algorithms but much more accurate.
MemeTracker MVC (Appendix C.1): S2V-DQN covers 474 nodes against an optimum of 473, ratio 1.0021; MVCApprox-Greedy 1.2220 and MVCApprox 1.4080 (Table 3, Section 5.4).
Ising MaxCut physics instances (Appendix C.2, Table C.1): ratio 1.0223 for S2V-DQN, optimal on 3 of 10 instances, versus 1.2825 for MaxcutApprox and 1.8996 for SDP (Table 3).
TSPLIB (Appendix C.3, Table C.2): S2V-DQN ratio 1.0475 across 38 instances with 51-318 cities, best tour on all but 6; next best Farthest 1.0800 and 2-opt 1.0947 (Table 3).
Set covering on MemeTracker-derived graphs (Appendix C.4): S2V-DQN ratio 1.001 versus LP 1.0009 and Greedy 1.03.

Discovered heuristics (Section 5.5, Appendix D.9-D.10): MVC picks nodes balancing degree against the connectivity of the remaining graph; MaxCut avoids adding nodes that cancel existing cut edges. Authors offer these as interpretable findings, not proofs.

PN-AC (pointer network, actor-critic) reproduces the Bello et al. TSP ratios only approximately: 1.03 vs 1.02 at TSP20, 1.07 vs 1.05 at TSP50, 1.09 vs 1.07 at TSP100 (Appendix D.11). Comparison is therefore sensitive to reimplementation.
Training convergence: MVC, MaxCut and SCP converge smoothly on validation; TSP is harder to learn from graph structure because the graph is fully connected (Appendix D.6, Figure D.2).
Sign of the TSP reward matters: the negative of the insertion reward worked better, which the authors explain as bias toward recent rewards (Appendix D.5).
limitations: Authors state the CPLEX 'optimal' values are often best-found solutions under a 1-hour cutoff, so ratios can fall below 1 or be inflated on large instances (Section 5.2, Appendix D.1).
TSP training is capped at 200-300 nodes by single-GPU memory; TSPLIB instances above 318 cities are not tackled (Appendix C.3).
Hyperparameters tuned only on graphs under 50 nodes and then fixed for larger graphs (Appendix D.4); MVC pre-training on smaller graphs is a heuristic trick (Section 5).
Reward design is described as still challenging; the sign-flip for TSP is ad hoc (Appendix D.5).
Speed comparison with GPU-based S2V-DQN against CPU-based baselines is acknowledged as not exactly fair (Section 5.3).
Dense graphs may need edge sampling for embedding computation; left as future work (Section 5.3).
No theoretical guarantees; the learned policy is empirical only.

summary_md: Dai, Khalil, Zhang, Dilkina and Song (NeurIPS 2017) learn greedy heuristics for NP-hard graph problems instead of hand-writing them. A structure2vec embedding (about 4-5 message-passing rounds, 64 dimensions) scores candidate nodes, and n-step Q-learning with fitted Q-iteration trains that score so a greedy loop adds one node at a time. Tested on minimum vertex cover, MaxCut, TSP and set cover, the learned policy (S2V-DQN) is near-optimal on synthetic graphs, holds up when trained on 50-100 nodes and run on 1000-1200 nodes (MVC ratio 1.0062), and beats hand heuristics on a 960-node MemeTracker diffusion graph (MVC ratio 1.0021 vs 1.2220 for greedy). It also wins on Ising MaxCut (1.0223) and TSPLIB (1.0475). Its edge is biggest where hand heuristics are weak (MVC, MaxCut). On set cover it nearly ties LP (1.001 vs 1.0009), and simple greedy trails by only 3 percent (1.03). extraction.research_question: Can a learned heuristic for budget-constrained set combinatorial problems on graphs (max coverage, max vertex cover, influence maximization) scale to billion-edge graphs while matching greedy and prior learned solvers in solution quality? (Sec 1, p.2-3)
extraction.theory: No formal economic or causal theory. Framework mixes supervised learning (GCN regresses probabilistic-greedy marginal-gain scores) with n-step fitted Q-learning over a state built from node score and locality (Eq 3: neighbors not already covered by the partial solution). Greedy 1-1/e approximation is cited from prior work (Sec 2, App B), not proved here.
extraction.data: SNAP graphs (Table 1a, p.6): Brightkite 58.2K nodes/214K edges; Gowalla 196.5K/950.3K; YouTube 1.13M/2.99M; StackOverflow 2.69M/5.9M; Orkut 3.07M/117.1M; Twitter 41.6M/1.5B; Friendster 65.6M/1.8B. Synthetic bipartite BP graphs (edge probability 0.1) and Barabasi-Albert graphs (density 4). Unit is the graph at budget b. IM edge weights: constant 0.1, tri-valency, or learned from Stack logs 8/2008-3/2016 (Sec 4.3, p.8).
extraction.method: Stage 1 (Sec 3.1-3.2, p.4-5): probabilistic greedy run m=30 times per graph, stopping at marginal gain 0.01, gives node scores (Eq 1). A noise predictor on the first GCN layer prunes low-rank nodes; a GCN (K=2, embedding 60, 1000 epochs) regresses scores by MSE on good nodes (Eq 2). Stage 2 (Sec 3.3, p.5): n-step fitted Q-learning (n=2, gamma 0.8) with max-pool state over good nodes; locality from importance-sampled neighbors (Theorem 1, App F). Inference: one GCN forward pass plus budget-many Q-steps. Baselines: S2V-DQN, GCN-TreeSearch, Greedy, CELF, CPLEX, IMM, OPIM.
extraction.scope: Set-valued, budget-constrained combinatorial problems on graphs only (MCP, MVC, IM); sequential and capacity-constrained problems explicitly excluded (Sec 5, p.9). Hardware: 64-core Xeon E5-2698v4, one GTX 1080 Ti (12 GB), 256 GB RAM, Ubuntu 16.04 (Sec 4.1, p.6). Era: 2020 NeurIPS benchmark on SNAP-scale graphs; no populations, institutions or time periods beyond the graph datasets.

key_findings.finding: Speed: GCOMB up to 2 orders of magnitude faster than GCN-TreeSearch and 10 times faster than Greedy on MCP (Twitter-ego, YouTube); speed-up over CELF on YouTube falls from 4.0 at b=20 to 2.01 at b=200.
Training time: GCOMB performance saturates within 10 minutes; S2V-DQN and GCN-TreeSearch need about 9 and 5 hours to reach best performance.
IM on YouTube subgraphs at b=20: GCN-TreeSearch takes about 3 hours on the 70 percent subgraph; GCOMB finishes in 5 seconds.

IM vs IMM on YouTube and Stack: GCOMB 30 to 160 times faster; spread difference entries in Table 3a are small (largest magnitude about 3e-3 at YT-TV, b=50). Units of the table entries are unclear given the x100 definition.
IMM crashes on Orkut, Twitter and Friendster (sample exceeds 256 GB RAM); GCOMB finishes within minutes for b<30 and within 100 minutes at b=100 and 200 on the billion-edge graphs.

Ablation: Q-learning adds up to 10 percent coverage over choosing top-b GCN scores on MCP; the noise predictor cuts running time by close to two orders of magnitude with no quality loss and slightly better quality.
Versus Stochastic Greedy: GCOMB up to 20 percent better quality at eps=0.2 and 2 times faster; Stochastic Greedy does not match GCOMB quality even at eps=0.05.

summary_md: GCOMB (Manchanda et al., NeurIPS 2020) learns a heuristic for budget-constrained set problems on graphs: max coverage, max vertex cover and influence maximization. A GCN regresses probabilistic-greedy marginal-gain scores; a noise predictor prunes low-value nodes; then n-step Q-learning picks seeds using score plus locality, the count of neighbours not already covered. The payoff is speed, not quality. On small graphs greedy already reaches at least 99 percent of the CPLEX optimum (BP-500 at b=20: GCOMB 0.998, greedy 0.99, optimal 1). On real graphs GCOMB matches greedy and runs about 10 times faster, 2 to 4 times faster than CELF on YouTube, and 30 to 160 times faster than IMM. It still finishes on billion-edge graphs where IMM runs out of 256 GB RAM. The paper explicitly excludes sequential and capacity-constrained problems (Sec 5). For Paul's systems, the dashboard's budget max-coverage recruiter is the direct descendant. It keeps GCOMB's locality idea (count only newly covered members) and a degree prune, but it uses exact greedy, which this paper's own evidence supports on a 533-member graph. The paper does not support replacing the CELF joint optimizer or the lazy-greedy frontier with a learned policy. Its gains appear only at million-edge scale. The optimizer's per-member PMAX cap is the capacity constraint GCOMB excludes. The IM objective is single-colour IC, evaluated with 10,000 Monte Carlo runs, not the system's two-colour competitive cascade at MC 20. An online scan found a 2024 VLDB benchmark (Liang et al., arXiv 2406.14697) reporting that lazy greedy consistently beats five deep-RL methods, GCOMB included, on max coverage. IMM and OPIM beat them on IM in most settings. That benchmark is not in the vault.
